reconcile.connective: Gill resolves the timing by distinguishing the tree's instant withering from the disciples' delayed discovery of it the next morning.

discrepancy.connective: D. F. Strauss argues Matthew's flat 'immediately' cannot honestly be harmonized by importing Mark's overnight gap into wording Matthew never wrote that way.

skeptic.name: David Friedrich Strauss
skeptic.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined
skeptic.attribution: D. F. Strauss (1808-1874), The Life of Jesus Critically Examined (1846)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The next day in the morning, as Mark says: they had, heard what Christ had said to it the day before, as the same evangelist observes; but did not take notice of the immediate withering of the tree; but the next morning, as they returned from Bethany, they saw it dried up from the roots:
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill directly harmonizes Matthew's instant withering with Mark's next-morning discovery by distinguishing the moment of withering (immediate) from the disciples' observation of it (delayed until the next morning).

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact passage, reconciling Matthew's 'presently' with Mark's next-morning notice by distinguishing the withering itself from the disciples' delayed observation of it.
